items.title: Anthropic Debuts on Nasdaq in Record $81.3B IPO, Briefly Topping $2 Trillion
items.summary: Anthropic began trading on Nasdaq under ticker ANT on 19 November after pricing its IPO at $83 a share - above the marketed $70-$78 range - and selling 980 million shares to raise $81.3 billion, the largest initial public offering on record. The stock opened at $111.50, 34% above the issue price, briefly pushing market capitalisation past $2 trillion before closing at $97.17, up 17%. Including a $26 billion private placement with AMD, Google, Microsoft, Nvidia and others, total fundraising exceeded $107 billion. Demand was roughly seven times the shares available. CEO Dario Amodei used the bell ceremony to pledge that Anthropic would pace AI training and deployment until systems are safe and remain under human control, as protesters gathered outside.
items.impact: As the first frontier AI lab to go public, Anthropic sets a market benchmark for an industry whose valuations have relied on private funding. The strong debut signals investor appetite despite a volatile week and Nvidia's leadership shock, but the gap between the $111.50 open and $97.17 close shows how fragile that confidence is. It also gives regulators and rivals a transparent view of AI economics for the first time.

items.title: Nvidia Revenue Doubles to $115.8B as AI Demand Fuels First $100B Quarter
items.summary: Nvidia reported fiscal 2027 third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% year on year and above the $109.3 billion consensus, marking its first quarter above $100 billion. Data-centre revenue climbed 110% to $107.6 billion, about 93% of the total, while GAAP diluted earnings per share doubled to $2.70 and net income reached roughly $65.3 billion. The company guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $130 billion, ahead of expectations, and said its Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale systems had begun shipping and were running on Oracle, Google Cloud, Azure, CoreWeave and Nebius. CFO Colette Kress, now interim CEO after Jensen Huang's resignation, raised the fiscal 2028 growth outlook to about 75%.
items.impact: The results are the clearest evidence yet that AI infrastructure spending remains robust even as investors question returns and new US rules restrict remote access to advanced chips. Nvidia's $2.5 trillion cloud-order backlog and 75% growth outlook will shape capex plans across hyperscalers and sovereign AI projects. The leadership transition now faces its real test: sustaining the roadmap and supplier relationships that underpin the AI build-out.

items.title: CISA Adds Four Exploited Flaws to KEV, Including Synology Ransomware Bug and LiteLLM AI Gateway
items.summary: CISA added four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 18 November, citing evidence of active exploitation. They are CVE-2024-10441 in Synology DiskStation Manager, an output-encoding flaw that C3RB3R ransomware has used to encrypt NAS devices running outdated DSM builds, leaving .L0CK3D files; CVE-2026-40217, an unprotected alternate-channel bug in BerriAI's LiteLLM AI gateway; CVE-2026-90436, an unsafe-reflection flaw in Apache Axis rated CVSS 9.8 that can be triggered by a crafted SOAP fault; and CVE-2026-90817, a code-injection flaw in Vanderbilt University's REDCap research data platform. Under BOD 26-04, federal agencies must remediate three by 21 November and LiteLLM by 2 December.
items.impact: The set shows attackers working both old and new surfaces: a two-year-old NAS bug now weaponised by ransomware, and LiteLLM, a gateway that stores AI provider keys, joining the list. Apache Axis was exploited just 12 days after disclosure, compressing the patch window. For defenders, KEV is no longer a technicality - it is the priority queue, and exposed management interfaces should be removed from the internet immediately.

items.title: Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Customers Hit by Third-Party Data Breach; n0n Ransomware Claims Credit
items.summary: A third-party service provider in the Asia-Pacific region was compromised, exposing customer data from Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase, according to a Wall Street Journal report cited by CNA on 20 November. Thousands of customers are affected. The ransomware group n0n claimed responsibility, but the companies said their own systems were not breached and services were uninterrupted. Visa said card numbers and payment data were not involved; Mastercard described a limited disclosure affecting some cardholders in a benefits programme; JPMorgan said attackers obtained marketing data that may include names and email addresses. Recorded Future analyst Andrei Barysevich said n0n targets firms with at least $10 million in revenue outside Russian-speaking countries.
items.impact: The incident underlines how payment and banking giants inherit risk through marketing and benefits vendors that sit outside their core security perimeter. Even without card data, exposed names and emails feed phishing and account-takeover campaigns. It will intensify scrutiny of fourth-party supply chains and validate demands for vendor inventory, access controls and breach-notification deadlines across the financial sector.

items.title: Irish DPC Fines Tinder EUR 11 Million Over Incomplete User Data Downloads
items.summary: Ireland's Data Protection Commission fined MTCH Technology Services, the operator of Tinder, EUR 11 million after an inquiry into how the dating app handles users' personal data requests, the EDPB announced on 17 November. The regulator found that Tinder's self-service 'Download My Data' tool omitted some personal data or supplied only summaries, and failed to alert users that the export was incomplete. Alongside the fine, the DPC issued a reprimand and ordered the company to bring its data-subject access process into compliance within three months. Match Group said it intends to appeal the decision.
items.impact: Access rights are the most exercised GDPR right, and regulators are now testing whether 'one-click' export tools actually deliver complete data. The ruling puts compliance teams on notice that partial exports and silent summaries count as failures, not good-faith approximations. It also signals continued EU focus on consumer apps, where data portability claims are easy to make and costly to substantiate.
